1:
The first thing the commentary has to settle is why Matthew has the centurion come in person while Luke has him send twice, and the answers differ in confidence. Henry disposes of it with a legal maxim, that what we do by another we are judged to do ourselves, so that the centurion did by his proxies what a man does by his attorney when he takes possession; and Henry thinks he probably came himself at last. Robertson offers the solution that Luke tells the story as it happened with the details while Matthew presents a summary without them, and quotes Plummer's judgment that Matthew puts the message of both embassies into the mouth of the centurion himself. Ellicott goes further and prefers Luke outright: the precision of his account leads us to receive it as the more accurate record, and it is also more true to nature, since the centurion was not likely to leave the slave who was so precious to him when he seemed in the very agonies of death. Bede explains the pattern from Luke's habit, which is to abridge or even purposely pass by whatever he sees plainly set forth by the other Evangelists, and to explain more carefully what they omit or touch briefly.

Ellicott then turns the argument against his own preference, which is the most interesting move in the passage. Luke here is, contrary to what we might have expected, less precise than Matthew, who states that the slave was sick of the palsy; and Ellicott asks whether the physician had been unable to satisfy himself from what he heard as to the nature of the disease. He notices too that the word rendered dear means precious, the dearness of value and not necessarily of affection, and that the elders are sent without the article, so that these are elders and not the whole body of them. Robertson fills in the military frame, that a centurion commanded a company varying from fifty to a hundred, six centuries making a cohort and ten cohorts a legion, and observes that the centurions named in the New Testament all seem to be fine men, Polybius having stated that the best men in the army held that position. He also holds that the opening verse really belongs as the conclusion of the previous chapter rather than the beginning of this one. On the synagogue Ellicott reads the article strictly, a well-known and conspicuous building and probably the only one in Capernaum, which he identifies with ruins lately discovered; Robertson notes only that the centurion built it all by himself and at his own expense.

On the centurion's word all the older voices fasten on one point. Chrysostom observes that he held a right opinion of the Lord, for he said not pray but command; and lest the Lord should from humility refuse him he added that he too was a man set under authority. Bede draws out the inference, that if a man subject to a tribune can command his inferiors, much more can he who is God fulfil whatever he wishes, not by the presence of his body only but by the services of his angels. Ambrose turns to the commendation and finds the Greek sharper than the English: read as not even in Israel have I found so great faith, this faith is preferred even to that of the more elect, those who see God. Bede narrows the comparison to the men of the present age rather than the patriarchs and prophets, because they were instructed in the precepts of the Law and the Prophets while the centurion, with no one to teach him, believed of his own accord. Ambrose closes on the servant, that the good deed of a master may advantage his servants not only through the merit of faith but through the practice of discipline.
11:
The Nain narrative is Luke's alone, and Ellicott argues carefully for its source. The city's name survives with hardly any alteration in the modern Nein, on the north-western edge of the Little Hermon where the ground falls into the plain of Esdraelon; the approach is a steep ascent and the rock on either side is full of sepulchral caves, and it was on the way to one of these that the procession was met. From that Ellicott infers that the miracle had specially fixed itself in the memories of the devout women named in the next chapter, and that Luke got his knowledge of it from them. He supports it from the wording: the narrative says when the Lord saw her, one of the few places where that term is used absolutely instead of the name, which fits a source that had learnt to speak of the Master so. Henry works instead on the attestation: the miracle was done in sight of two crowds meeting at the gate, one of disciples following Jesus and one of relations and neighbours following the bier, so that there was a sufficient number to attest it; and reckons the raising a greater proof of divine authority than the healings, since by no power of nature can the dead be raised.

On the grief itself Henry and Ellicott divide the labour. Henry dwells on the loss: the mother had depended on her son as the staff of her old age and he proved a broken reed, as every man at his best estate is, and being a widow she was broken with breach upon breach; he adds that the young man was cut off in the beginning of his days, since man comes forth like a flower and is cut down, and calls the world for such sufferers a vale of tears and a place of weepers. Ellicott keeps to the facts, that an only son and a widowed mother enhance the bitterness and that burial took place outside the city as was invariable, and that the mother, probably following at some distance among the mourners, received her son as given to her once again in a higher sense than when she had rejoiced that a man-child was born. Bede fixes the place, a city of Galilee within two miles of Mount Tabor, and finds a providence in the crowd, since by divine counsel large multitudes accompanied the Lord that there might be many witnesses of so great a miracle.

Titus anticipates the objection that the centurion's servant was not going to die, and says the Evangelist forestalls it by making plain that this young man was already dead. He also measures the act against the precedents and finds none of them adequate: the Saviour is not like Elijah mourning over the son of the widow of Sarepta, nor Elisha who laid his own body on the body of the dead, nor Peter who prayed for Tabitha, but is none other than he who calls those things which be not as though they were. Cyril fastens on the touch, that the miracle was performed not only in word but by touching the bier, so that we might know the body of Christ is powerful to save; as iron applied to fire does the work of fire, so the flesh united to the Word becomes itself quickening and the banisher of death. Ellicott supplies what was touched, not a closed coffin like the mummy cases of Egypt but an open bier with the corpse in its winding sheet and a napkin laid lightly over the face, and observes that the bearers must have marvelled that a known Teacher should touch what most Rabbis would have avoided as pollution. Bede glosses the command not to weep as meaning cease to weep for one as dead whom you shall soon see rise again alive.
19:
Why the Baptist sent at all is handled gently by everyone. Henry puts the need for confirmation on John's disciples as much as on John, and explains it from the circumstances: Christ had not yet publicly declared himself, would not have those who knew him speak of it until the proofs were completed in his resurrection, the great men of the Jewish church had not owned him, and nothing of the expected Messianic grandeur was to be seen about him. Cyril sees the Lord forestalling a harsher inference, that if John were ignorant of Jesus until now his earlier pointing him out as the Lamb of God was worthless; the discourse that follows is placed to quench that feeling before it could do injury. Christ left it to his own works to praise him in the gates, Henry adds, and Ellicott notices that the statement of cures wrought in that same hour is peculiar to Luke and adds much force, since he pointed to what was passing before the questioners' eyes. Ellicott also notes that Luke alone gives the number of disciples sent, and that the best manuscripts have them sent to the Lord.

On the praise of John the older voices work the reed hardest. Cyril glosses it as a rebuke to the crowd's own suspicion: you crossed long journeys into the desert to see him, in vain if you now think him so fickle as to bend whichever way the wind moves, which is how a man appears who lightly avows ignorance of what he knows. Titus makes the same point from the geography, that they left their cities for a desert where there is no pleasantness and can only have done it out of care for this man; and on the title of messenger he is precise, that John is called an angel not by nature, being by nature a man, but because he exercised the office in heralding the advent. Ambrose praises the character rather than the office, that John preferred the way of righteousness to the love of life and swerved not through fear of death, and turns the reed into an allegory of the world as a desert where men puffed up with a fleshly mind and vaunting themselves in frail glory are tossed about by a restless life. Greater than a prophet, he says, was he in whom the prophets terminate, for many desired to see him whom John saw and baptized. Ellicott finds Luke's gorgeously apparelled more vivid than Matthew's soft clothing, bringing out ostentatious display and effeminate self-indulgence common in the house of Herod, and traces a touch of brutal vindictiveness in the bright robe those same Herodians afterwards put upon the Prophet of Nazareth.

Calvin takes the two classes that Matthew omits and makes them the hinge. The passage throws no small light on the connection, since the obstinacy of the scribes in despising God gave rise to the expostulation; and he reads the Lord as intending from the beginning to hold out this example, that neither that age nor posterity might judge the Gospel by the approbation of men. Ellicott thinks it interposed for Gentile readers, to show the preaching's effect on two classes at opposite extremes of the nation's life, and would render the first clause acknowledged God as righteous and the second, against the unhappy ambiguity of the English, frustrated for themselves the counsel of God. On the children's song Calvin is sharpest: Christ borrowed from children the materials of his reproof, so that nothing more was needed to condemn the scribes, however distinguished, than a song children sang in the market-place for their amusement. John sang a plaintive song and the Lord a cheerful one and neither succeeded; and against those who place the highest perfection in outward austerity Calvin observes that on that principle John would rank higher than the Son of God.
36:
Who the woman was divides the passage, and Ellicott settles it by refusing it. The widespread belief that she was Mary Magdalene has absolutely not a single jot or tittle of evidence in Scripture, nor anything like a tradition in its favour; the earliest Fathers are silent, it was discussed and rejected early, Ambrose and Augustine are doubtful, and it first gained acceptance through the authority of Gregory, afterwards stamped by the choice of this narrative for her feast. Henry reaches the same verdict by another argument: the identification is commonly made but he finds no ground in Scripture for it, and the Magdalene is described elsewhere as one out of whom seven devils were cast, which is not mentioned here, so probably it was not she. Ambrose keeps the harder question, how this anointing relates to Matthew's. Matthew has the ointment poured on the head and was therefore unwilling to call the woman a sinner, while here the sinner anoints the feet; so she cannot be the same, lest the Evangelists seem at variance, though Ambrose allows the difficulty may also be solved by a difference of merit and of time, the former still a sinner and the latter now more perfect. Augustine resolves it the other way, that the same Mary did this twice, once as Luke relates, coming with humility and weeping and thought worthy of forgiveness, and again at Bethany in the occurrence the other three record.

On the Pharisee the commentary is severe, and Ellicott reconstructs the slight. There had been no real respect in the invitation, which was hardly more than ostentatious patronage; the courtesies due to well-nigh every guest, which a Rabbi might expect as a thing of course, were in his judgment superfluous, and Simon may already have heard that the new Teacher cared little for ablutions and seen no point providing them. He fills in each omitted courtesy: the kiss, a customary mark of respect to a Rabbi that became the kiss of peace in the Liturgies, and the anointing of the head, less common but still due to an honoured guest and a comfort to one who had journeyed under the burning sun of Syria; and he marks the contrast between olive oil and the costlier ointment. Henry notes that the Pharisee did not believe in Christ, since he will not own him a prophet, and that Christ accepted the invitation anyway, taking the same liberty with Pharisees as with publicans in hopes of doing them good. Ellicott observes that Simon, like the woman of Samaria, located the prophetic character not in prediction but in the power to read the secrets of men's hearts, and detects a tone of satisfaction at having caught out an inconsistency.

The parable's logic produces the chapter's firmest cross-tradition agreement. Calvin holds its whole scope is to show Simon wrong in condemning a woman whom the heavenly judge acquits, and will not let love be the price: the argument is taken not from the cause but from the effect, since until a favour has been received it cannot awaken gratitude, and the cause of reciprocal love is declared to be a free forgiveness. He calls it a gross blunder that most commentators have made the woman earn her pardon. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by grammar, granting the words admit two interpretations equally tenable but holding the whole drift of the parable in favour of love as the consequence of forgiveness rather than its ground, and noting that the later absolution did not convey forgiveness for the first time but came to banish every lingering doubt. Gregory reads the ointment as the sweet savour of a good report, so that good works sprinkle the Church with it; and Calvin finds the exposure of Simon's silent thought meant to assure us all that no sinner need fear rejection by one who invites with outstretched arms.
